Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.h: Bank M02 — Helix Composites: break-even with a discount for one customer
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of Exercise 1 of the examples PDF (Pegasus S.A.). Differences: the commercial discount applies only to part of the customers, the cost list contains an item that is not an operating cost, the profit target is a margin on sales, and the price is cut instead of raised. Method: Topic 4, Slides 37 to 42; price elasticity from Topic 5, Slide 17 and topic 5.2.2.pdf, pp. 2-3.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
Helix Composites S.L. manufactures carbon-fibre rotor blades for cargo drones. Its expected annual costs are:

- Lease of the autoclave hall: 380,000 €
- Salaries of the lay-up operators, hired on fixed annual contracts: 460,000 €
- Salaries of the engineering and quality staff: 200,000 €
- Depreciation of the moulds and the autoclave: 100,000 €
- Insurance and administration: 60,000 €
- Interest on the bank loan that financed the autoclave: 60,000 €
- Carbon prepreg and resin: 36 € per blade
- Autoclave energy: 7 € per blade
- Packaging and transport to the customer: 5 € per blade

The sales forecast is 25,000 blades a year. 40% of the blades are sold to one drone manufacturer (OEM) under a framework contract that gives it a 10% discount on the list price; the other customers buy the remaining 60% at the list price.

a) Classify the costs and calculate the list price per blade that makes the firm break even (zero operating profit) at the forecast volume of 25,000 blades. (0.5 points)

b) Using the list price found in (a), calculate the volume of blades the firm must sell to earn an operating profit equal to 10% of its net sales revenue. (0.5 points)

c) Calculate the operating leverage (OL) at the volume found in (b) and at a volume of 40,000 blades. What do these values mean? (0.75 points)

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x: d) At 40,000 blades the price elasticity of demand is 1.5. The firm cuts its list price by 4%, keeping the OEM discount and the share of each group of customers. Calculate the new expected volume, the new operating profit and the change in sales revenue, and explain the result. (0.75 points)

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
| Item | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Forecast volume | $Q = 25{,}000$ blades |
| Share of the OEM (10% discount) | 40% of the units |
| Share of the other customers (list price) | 60% of the units |
| Target of part (b) | operating profit = 10% of net sales revenue |
| Second volume of part (c) | 40,000 blades |
| Price elasticity at 40,000 blades | $E_d = 1.5$ (absolute value) |
| Change of the list price in part (d) | −4% |

Model of the course:

- Profit $= P\,Q - (VC\,Q + FC) = Q\,(P - VC) - FC$, unit margin $m = P - VC$, break-even point $Q_0 = FC/m$ (Topic 4, Slide 37).
- Operating leverage $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC) = Q/(Q - Q^*)$ (Topic 4, Slides 39, 40 and 42).
- Price elasticity $E_d = (\Delta Q/Q)/(\Delta P/P)$, used in absolute value, so $\Delta Q/Q = -E_d\,\Delta P/P$ (Topic 5, Slide 17; topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2), as in Examples PDF, Exercise 1 (d).

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x: A cost is fixed when its yearly amount does not depend on the number of blades. Revenue is earned at the average net price that the two groups of customers pay, not at the list price. Ask whether the interest on the loan is an operating cost.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
- $FC$ = 1,200,000 €; $VC$ = 48 € per blade; the interest (60,000 €) is not an operating cost
- Average net price = 0.96 × list price
- Net price = 96 € per blade; list price = 100 € per blade

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
#### Classify the costs

The lease, the salaries of the operators (fixed annual contracts, as the direct labour of Examples PDF, Exercise 1), the salaries of the engineering and quality staff, the depreciation and the insurance and administration are the same whatever the number of blades: they are fixed costs.

$$FC = 380{,}000 + 460{,}000 + 200{,}000 + 100{,}000 + 60{,}000 = 1{,}200{,}000\ \text{€}$$

The prepreg and resin, the energy of the autoclave and the packaging and transport are spent once per blade: they are variable costs per unit.

$$VC = 36 + 7 + 5 = 48\ \text{€/blade}$$

The interest on the bank loan is a financial expense, a non-operating item of the income statement (Topic 3, Slide 11): it lies below the operating profit (EBIT) and does not enter a break-even point defined on the operating profit. It is left out of $FC$.

#### Average net price

Of every 100 blades, 40 are sold at $0.90\,P_L$ (list price minus the 10% discount) and 60 at $P_L$. The average net price per blade is the weighted mean:

$$P = 0.40 \times 0.90\,P_L + 0.60 \times P_L = (0.36 + 0.60)\,P_L = 0.96\,P_L$$

#### Break-even condition at 25,000 blades

At the break-even point revenue equals total cost, $P\,Q_0 = FC + VC\,Q_0$ (Topic 4, Slide 37). Solving for the net price:

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
$$P = \frac{FC + VC\,Q_0}{Q_0} = \frac{1{,}200{,}000 + 48 \times 25{,}000}{25{,}000} = \frac{2{,}400{,}000}{25{,}000} = 96\ \text{€/blade}$$

#### From the net price to the list price

$$P_L = \frac{P}{0.96} = \frac{96}{0.96} = 100\ \text{€/blade}$$

Check: $m = 96 - 48 = 48$ € and $Q_0 = FC/m = 1{,}200{,}000/48 = 25{,}000$ blades, the forecast volume. Units: € divided by € per blade gives blades. Had the interest been counted as a fixed cost, the net price would be $(1{,}260{,}000 + 1{,}200{,}000)/25{,}000 = 98.4$ € and the list price 102.5 €; had the discount been applied to all customers, as in Pegasus, the list price would be $96/0.90 = 106.67$ €.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x: Write the target as an equation in $Q$: the profit $Q\,m - FC$ must equal 10% of the revenue $P\,Q$. The target profit is not a fixed number, so $Q = (\text{Profit} + FC)/m$ cannot be used directly.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
- Unit margin $m$ = 48 € per blade, 10% of the net price = 9.60 € per blade
- $Q$ = 31,250 blades
- Revenue 3,000,000 €, operating profit 300,000 €

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
#### Set the target as an equation

With the list price of 100 €, the net price is $P = 96$ € and $m = P - VC = 96 - 48 = 48$ € per blade. The target is

$$Q\,m - FC = 0.10 \times P\,Q$$

#### Solve for the volume

Move the terms in $Q$ to the left and factor $Q$:

$$Q\,(m - 0.10\,P) = FC \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = \frac{FC}{m - 0.10\,P} = \frac{1{,}200{,}000}{48 - 0.10 \times 96} = \frac{1{,}200{,}000}{38.40} = 31{,}250\ \text{blades}$$

Each blade leaves 48 € of margin, of which 9.60 € must be kept as profit, so only 38.40 € per blade is left to cover the fixed costs.

#### Check

Revenue $= 96 \times 31{,}250 = 3{,}000{,}000$ €. Operating profit $= 31{,}250 \times 48 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 1{,}500{,}000 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 300{,}000$ €, which is $300{,}000/3{,}000{,}000 = 10\%$ of the revenue. The volume is above the break-even point (25,000 blades), as a positive profit requires.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
- At 31,250 blades: $Q\,m$ = 1,500,000 €, profit 300,000 €, OL = 5.00
- At 40,000 blades: $Q\,m$ = 1,920,000 €, profit 720,000 €, OL = 2.67
- Meaning: a 1% change in sales changes the operating profit by 5% and by 2.67%

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
#### Leverage at 31,250 blades

$$OL = \frac{Q\,m}{Q\,m - FC} = \frac{31{,}250 \times 48}{31{,}250 \times 48 - 1{,}200{,}000} = \frac{1{,}500{,}000}{300{,}000} = 5.00$$

Check with the break-even point, $Q^* = 25{,}000$ (Topic 4, Slide 42): $OL = 31{,}250/(31{,}250 - 25{,}000) = 31{,}250/6{,}250 = 5.00$.

#### Leverage at 40,000 blades

$$OL = \frac{40{,}000 \times 48}{40{,}000 \times 48 - 1{,}200{,}000} = \frac{1{,}920{,}000}{720{,}000} = 2.67$$

Check: $OL = 40{,}000/(40{,}000 - 25{,}000) = 40{,}000/15{,}000 = 2.67$.

#### Meaning

The OL measures how a change in sales translates into a change in operating profit (Topic 4, Slide 40). At 31,250 blades a 1% change in sales changes the operating profit by 5% in the same direction (a 10% fall in sales would cut profit by 50%); at 40,000 blades the same 1% changes the profit by only 2.67%. Both values are greater than 1 because the firm has profits ($Q > Q^*$), and the leverage falls as the volume moves away from the break-even point (Topic 4, Slide 42). The OL is an index of economic risk (Topic 4, Slide 41): Helix is riskier at 31,250 blades, close to its break-even point, than at 40,000. The leverage is a pure number: € over €, or blades over blades.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x: Because the discount is a percentage and the customer mix does not change, the average net price falls by the same 4% as the list price. Apply $\Delta Q/Q = -E_d\,\Delta P/P$ at the starting point of 40,000 blades, then recompute margin and profit.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
- $\Delta Q/Q$ = +6%, new volume 42,400 blades
- New net price 92.16 €, new margin 44.16 €
- New operating profit 672,384 € (was 720,000 €: −47,616 €)
- Revenue rises from 3,840,000 € to 3,907,584 € (+67,584 €)

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x:
#### New volume

The relative change of the list price is $\Delta P/P = -4\% = -0.04$. With $E_d = 1.5$ in absolute value (Topic 5, Slide 17; topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2):

$$\frac{\Delta Q}{Q} = -E_d\,\frac{\Delta P}{P} = -1.5 \times (-0.04) = +0.06$$

$$Q_{new} = 40{,}000 \times (1 + 0.06) = 42{,}400\ \text{blades}$$

#### New net price and margin

The average net price is $0.96\,P_L$, so it changes in the same proportion as the list price:

$$P_{new} = 96 \times (1 - 0.04) = 92.16\ \text{€/blade} \qquad m_{new} = 92.16 - 48 = 44.16\ \text{€/blade}$$

(New list price $100 \times 0.96 = 96$ €; $0.96 \times 96 = 92.16$ €, the same result.)

#### New operating profit

$$\text{Profit}_{new} = Q_{new}\,m_{new} - FC = 42{,}400 \times 44.16 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 1{,}872{,}384 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 672{,}384\ \text{€}$$

Before the price cut: $\text{Profit} = 40{,}000 \times 48 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 720{,}000$ €. The profit falls by $720{,}000 - 672{,}384 = 47{,}616$ €.

#### Revenue and explanation

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x: Revenue before: $40{,}000 \times 96 = 3{,}840{,}000$ €. Revenue after: $42{,}400 \times 92.16 = 3{,}907{,}584$ €, a rise of 67,584 €. The demand is elastic ($E_d > 1$), so a price cut raises the volume more than proportionally and the revenue rises (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 3). The operating profit, however, falls: the unit margin drops from 48 € to 44.16 €, a fall of $3.84/48 = 8\%$, twice the 4% price cut because the variable cost does not fall, and the 6% gain in volume does not make up for it. Higher revenue does not mean higher profit; the decision must be judged on the margin.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
chunks.x: Helix's break-even list price (100 €) already includes the fact that only 40% of the blades carry the discount, which lowers the average price by 4% instead of 10%. The leverage falls from 5.00 to 2.67 as the firm moves from 31,250 to 40,000 blades, so further away from its break-even point its profit is less sensitive to sales. The price cut of part (d) is the opposite of the price rise of Pegasus: with elastic demand it gains revenue but loses operating profit, because each blade sold earns 3.84 € less while the fixed costs stay at 1,200,000 €. Limiting cases: with no OEM customers the factor 0.96 becomes 1 and the list price would be 96 €; at $Q = Q^* = 25{,}000$ the OL is not defined (the profit is zero). Dimensions: prices and margins in € per blade, volumes in blades, profits and revenues in €, OL and elasticity dimensionless.

chunks.t: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a
VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.h: Bank M03 — VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of Exercise 2 of the examples PDF (TechNova Solutions). The company is invented. Concepts: Topic 5, Slides 6-14 (strategic marketing, segmentation, positioning), 19-24 (product attributes and range of products) and 34-37 (distribution); Examples PDF, Exercise 2.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
VectraSky is a Portuguese company founded in 2016 in Porto that designs and builds small fixed-wing drones for surveying crops and forests. Before launching its first model, the founders studied the drone market and its competitors: the large manufacturers were focused on hobby users and film-makers, while medium-sized farms and forestry cooperatives in southern Europe had no affordable aircraft able to survey a whole estate in one flight. VectraSky decided to serve only these farms and cooperatives, and its slogan, "The whole farm on one charge", presents its drones as the long-endurance option at a moderate price.

The drones carry the VectraSky name and a green swallow as logo. The wings fold so that the aircraft fits in the boot of a car, it is ready to fly in under five minutes, and it is flown from a tablet application with large buttons that can be used with work gloves. Every airframe is sealed against dust and rain and is flown for 20 hours in the factory before delivery, and the drone comes with a three-year warranty. It is delivered in a rugged, reusable transport case whose label gives the operating instructions in four languages. After the sale, VectraSky ships any spare part within 48 hours and trains the customer's pilots on site. To make itself known, the firm runs flight demonstrations at agricultural fairs and places advertisements in farming magazines.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
The current range has two product lines: survey drones (Field 60, Field 90 and Forest 120) and sensor payloads (a multispectral camera and a thermal camera); every product is used for the aerial survey of crops and forests. VectraSky does not sell to its customers directly: its drones are sold by agricultural-machinery dealers, who resell them to the farms and cooperatives. The firm chooses at most two dealers in each region, and only dealers that have a workshop able to repair the drones.

a) Which elements of the strategic marketing approach appear in the text? Identify at least three and justify each with a fact of the text. (0.75 points)

b) Which product attribute strategy does VectraSky follow? Identify at least four attributes, and say which facts of the text are not product attributes. (0.75 points)

c) Describe the range of products of VectraSky (extension or width, depth, length and consistency), and say which characteristics change if the firm adds a Field 75 model to its drone line. (0.5 points)

d) Which distribution strategy does VectraSky follow? Describe the type and length of the channel, whether it is B2B or B2C, and the distribution intensity. (0.5 points)

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x: Strategic marketing is the analysis system: analysis of the situation, diagnosis, objective, and the strategies of segmentation and positioning. Look in the first paragraph for each of them.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
- Analysis of the situation: market and competitors' analysis (the founders "studied the drone market and its competitors").
- Market segmentation and targeting: medium-sized farms and forestry cooperatives in southern Europe, a single segment (differentiated concentrated, niche strategy), identified as an unmet need.
- Positioning: "The whole farm on one charge", long endurance at a moderate price (benefits of the product, price-quality relationship).
- Customer orientation (market orientation): the product is designed for the needs of the chosen customers.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
#### Analysis of the situation

"The founders studied the drone market and its competitors": this is the first stage of strategic marketing, the analysis of the situation (market analysis and competitors' analysis) [Topic 5, Slide 7]. The finding that the large manufacturers left farms and cooperatives without an affordable long-endurance aircraft is an opportunity in the sense of the slide: segmentation identifies the market needs that are not being satisfied [Topic 5, Slide 11].

#### Market segmentation and targeting

"Medium-sized farms and forestry cooperatives in southern Europe" defines a segment with a geographical criterion (southern Europe) and a criterion of type of use of the product (surveying crops and forests) [Topic 5, Slide 10]. "VectraSky decided to serve only these farms and cooperatives": the firm aims its product and its message at a single, well-defined segment, the differentiated concentrated (niche) strategy [Topic 5, Slide 12].

#### Positioning

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
"The whole farm on one charge ... the long-endurance option at a moderate price" is the image the firm wants to create in the mind of the target customer: positioning [Topic 5, Slide 13]. It is based on a benefit of the product (surveying a whole estate in one flight) and on the price-quality relationship [Topic 5, Slide 14]. Positioning is a strategic decision, not an operative one [Examples PDF, Exercise 4, statement 1].

#### Customer orientation

The whole offer starts from what the chosen customers need, which is the market (customer) orientation of the active marketing stage: producing what potential customers want [Topic 5, Slide 4]. Three of these four elements, each with its fact of the text, earn the full marks.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x: The psychosocial attributes of the product are brand, design, packaging and quality; warranty and post-sale service are further attributes. Promotion is a different element of the marketing mix.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
- Brand: name VectraSky and a green swallow as logo.
- Design: folding wings, fits in a car boot, ready in under five minutes, tablet application usable with gloves (aesthetic and functional).
- Quality: sealed against dust and rain, 20 hours of factory flight before delivery.
- Packaging: rugged reusable transport case with the instructions in four languages on its label.
- Warranty and post-sale service: three-year warranty, spare parts in 48 hours, on-site pilot training.
- Not product attributes: flight demonstrations at fairs and advertisements in farming magazines belong to the promotion (communication) policy.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
#### The attributes found in the text

The product is a bundle of tangible and intangible attributes; besides the basic product the customer buys quality, design, packaging, post-sale services and image, and the psychosocial attributes are brand, design, packaging and quality [Topic 5, Slide 19].

| Fact of the text | Attribute of the course |
| :--- | :--- |
| "The VectraSky name and a green swallow as logo" | Brand: a name (the part that can be said) and a logo (design, symbol, colours) [Topic 5, Slide 20] |
| "The wings fold ... fits in the boot of a car ... ready to fly in under five minutes ... large buttons that can be used with work gloves" | Design, from the functional perspective of ease of use [Topic 5, Slide 22] |
| "Sealed against dust and rain ... flown for 20 hours in the factory before delivery" | Quality: the product satisfies the needs of customers who fly in the field [Topic 5, Slide 23] |
| "Rugged, reusable transport case whose label gives the operating instructions in four languages" | Packaging: it protects the content, eases transport and carries the label with information [Topic 5, Slide 22] |
| "Three-year warranty ... spare part within 48 hours ... trains the customer's pilots on site" | Warranty and post-sale services [Topic 5, Slide 23] |

Four of these attributes, each with its fact, earn the full marks.

#### What is not a product attribute

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x: "Flight demonstrations at agricultural fairs" and "advertisements in farming magazines" are not attributes of the product: they belong to the promotion (communication) policy of the marketing mix, the first as an activity close to personal selling and public relations at the fairs, the second as advertising, a paid, non-personal communication through the mass media [Topic 5, Slides 29-30]. The examples PDF draws the same line: communication is not a product attribute [Examples PDF, Exercise 2 (b)].

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x: Count the lines, the products in each line and the products in total. Then ask which of the counts a new model inside an existing line changes.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
- Extension (width): 2 lines.
- Depth: 3 drones and 2 payloads.
- Length: 5 products.
- Consistency: high, every product serves the aerial survey of crops and forests.
- Field 75: depth of the drone line 3 to 4, length 5 to 6; extension (width) and consistency unchanged.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
#### Characteristics of the current range

A range of products is an offer of product lines and individual products, described by its extension, depth, length and consistency [Topic 5, Slide 24]. The examples PDF calls the extension the width (breadth) of the range [Examples PDF, Exercise 4, statement 3].

| Characteristic | Definition | VectraSky |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Extension (width) | number of product lines | 2 (survey drones, sensor payloads) |
| Depth | number of products per line | 3 drones; 2 payloads |
| Length | total number of individual products | $3 + 2 = 5$ |
| Consistency | relation of the products with their final use | high: every product is used "for the aerial survey of crops and forests" |

#### A Field 75 model

The Field 75 enters the existing drone line, which is the strategy "extend the product lines" [Topic 5, Slide 24]: the depth of the drone line rises from 3 to 4 and the length of the range from 5 to 6. The extension (width) stays at 2, because no new line is created, and the consistency stays high, because the new drone has the same final use.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x: Ask who sells to the final buyer, how many intermediaries stand between the producer and that buyer, whether the buyer is a firm or a consumer, and how many outlets there are in each region.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
- Indirect channel: independent agricultural-machinery dealers.
- Short channel with one level of intermediaries: producer, dealer, farm.
- B2B: the final buyers are farms and cooperatives, which are firms.
- Selective intensity: at most two chosen dealers per region, with a repair workshop.

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x:
#### Type and length of the channel

"VectraSky does not sell to its customers directly: its drones are sold by agricultural-machinery dealers": the producer entrusts the sale to independent intermediaries, so the channel is indirect [Topic 5, Slide 35]. One intermediary stands between the producer and the final buyer (producer, dealer, farm), a short channel of one level. Extension: the level of a channel is the number of intermediaries between the producer and the final buyer; the examples PDF calls a channel with none a zero-level channel [Examples PDF, Exercise 2 (c)].

#### B2B and intensity

The final buyers, farms and forestry cooperatives, are firms, so the market is business-to-business (B2B), as in the TechNova case [Examples PDF, Exercise 2 (c)]. "At most two dealers in each region, and only dealers that have a workshop able to repair the drones" is selective distribution, one of the three strategies of Slide 37 [Topic 5, Slide 37]. Extension (definitions not given on the slide): intensive distribution uses as many outlets as possible, selective distribution a limited number of chosen outlets per area, and exclusive distribution a single outlet per area. The workshop requirement shows the criteria of the choice: the characteristics of the product (it needs repairs) and of each intermediary [Topic 5, Slide 37].

chunks.t: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
chunks.x: Every decision of VectraSky follows from its strategic choice. A single segment (farms and cooperatives that survey large areas) explains the long-endurance design, the rugged case and the field service; a short, selective channel of dealers with workshops keeps that service close to the customer without the cost of an own sales network.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.h: Bank M04 — Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Case written for the bank in the style of Exercise 3 of the examples PDF (managerial functions, decision-making process, KPIs and organizational configuration). The firm is fictitious. Content: Topic 6, Slides 3-8, 13-16, 18, 20 and 22-25. KPIs are not defined in the Topic 6 deck: they are taken from Examples PDF, Exercise 3, and treated as an **extension**.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
Altair MRO is a maintenance, repair and overhaul company with 600 employees and three hangars that service regional aircraft. Today every inspection and repair is recorded on paper task cards; the cards travel by hand to the planning office, aircraft often leave the hangar late because a card or a spare part is missing, and the airlines that are its customers complain that they only learn about delays at the last minute.

The Chief Executive Officer wants to replace the paper cards with a **digital maintenance platform**: technicians would record each task on a tablet at the aircraft, the stock of spare parts would update automatically, and the airline would follow the progress of its aircraft online. The firm has never used such a system and no competitor of its size has one. The firm is organized by functions (inspection, repair, planning, stores), each with its own head; every procedure is written in detailed manuals, there are six hierarchical levels between the technician and the CEO, and any change to a procedure must be approved by the technical director.

Tasks:

a) Describe at least one task that should be performed in each of the four managerial functions to introduce the platform. (0.5 points)

b) List the steps of the decision-making process the CEO should follow, applying each one to the case. (0.5 points)

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
c) Classify the decision to adopt the platform by type of decision and by management level, and say which basic managerial skill weighs most for the manager who takes it. (0.5 points)

d) Define four KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) to control the introduction of the platform. (0.5 points)

e) Using the basic organizational configurations of Mintzberg, state in which one the platform would be hardest to introduce and in which one easiest, justifying each answer with the features of the configuration. (0.5 points)

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x: The four functions of the course are planning, organizing, leading and controlling. In the course, leading is human resources management (directing and staffing), and controlling measures results against the standards set when planning.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
- Planning: objectives and calendar of the roll-out (goal with a date, forecasts, alternatives, chosen course of action).
- Organizing: who does what, a project team, new tasks and their coordination, the organization chart updated.
- Leading: motivation, communication and training of technicians; recruiting and selecting new profiles if needed.
- Controlling: standards, measurement, deviations, corrective action.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
#### Planning

Planning is setting goals and deciding on the strategy to achieve them, and a goal is a specific achievement to be attained at a future date (Topic 6, Slide 10). Task: set the objective "all three hangars working without paper task cards within twelve months", forecast the cost and the training time, compare a gradual roll-out (one hangar first) with a simultaneous one, and fix the calendar of the chosen option.

#### Organizing

Organizing arranges the human resources so that their activities contribute to the firm's goals, through differentiation (dividing the work) and integration (coordinating it) (Topic 6, Slide 11). Task: create a project team with members of inspection, repair, planning and stores, give each member a distinct task (data migration, tablet set-up, rewriting the procedures), name one person per hangar to coordinate, and update the organization chart with the new roles.

#### Leading

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
Leading is human resources management (Topic 6, Slides 2 and 23): directing (motivation, leadership, communication) and staffing (recruiting, selecting, training, appraisal and compensation). Task: explain to the technicians why the paper cards are being replaced, train every technician on the tablets, and recruit and then select a data specialist if nobody in the firm can run the platform. Recruitment (attracting candidates) comes before selection (choosing among them).

#### Controlling

Controlling ensures that activities provide the planned results: establishing standards, measuring actual performance, identifying deviations and taking corrective action (Topic 6, Slide 24). Task: compare every month the progress of the roll-out with the calendar set when planning, measure the KPIs of part (d), and correct the deviations (more training in a hangar that lags behind, for example). Buying the tablets is an operation of the project, not a managerial function in itself.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
- The eight steps in the order of the course, each applied to Altair MRO.
- Analysis (step 4) before choice (step 5); evaluation (step 7) before changes (step 8).

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
#### The eight steps in the case

The decision-making process has eight steps (Topic 6, Slide 6):

1. **Recognizing the problem or opportunity:** aircraft leave late because paper cards and spare parts go missing, and customers learn about delays at the last minute.
2. **Gathering information, identifying the critical factors:** how many delays come from lost cards or missing parts, how many technicians and aircraft are involved, the budget, and what the airlines expect.
3. **Considering alternative courses of action:** keep paper but add a courier between hangar and office; scan the cards at the end of each shift; adopt the full digital platform.
4. **Analysing the alternatives:** cost, time to introduce, training needed and expected reduction of delays of each one.
5. **Choosing an alternative:** the digital platform, the only one that updates stock and informs the customer in real time.
6. **Implementing the decision:** the roll-out planned and organized in part (a).
7. **Evaluating the results:** compare delays and customer complaints before and after, with the KPIs of part (d).
8. **Implementing changes:** adjust the platform, the procedures or the training where the evaluation shows deviations.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x: Slide 5 classifies decisions by the type of problem and of alternatives; Slide 7 places the decisions on the management pyramid; Slide 8 shows which skill weighs most at each level.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
- Innovative (not planned) decision: new and ambiguous problem, unplanned alternatives; quote "never used such a system", "no competitor of its size".
- Top management, strategic and general decision.
- Conceptual skill, the ability to see the firm as a whole.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
#### Type of decision

The firm "has never used such a system and no competitor of its size has one": the problem is unusual and the alternatives are ambiguous and not planned, so this is an **innovative (not planned) decision**, not a routine one, which would face a known, well-defined problem with known alternatives (Topic 6, Slide 5).

#### Management level

The platform changes the way the three hangars, the stores and the relation with the customers work: it affects the firm as a whole, so it is a **strategic, general** decision of **top management** (the CEO), not a tactical decision of middle management or an operational one of first-line supervisors (Topic 6, Slide 7; Examples PDF, Exercise 4, statement 5). Choosing which hangar team is trained first on Monday would, by contrast, be an operational decision.

#### Skill

The skill that weighs most in top management is the **conceptual skill**, the ability to see the firm as a whole: the CEO must see how the platform links maintenance, stores, planning and customers. Technical skill weighs most in low management (Topic 6, Slide 8).

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x: A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is a measurable indicator of whether an objective is being achieved; it is the measure of actual performance that controlling compares with a standard. The term is not defined in the Topic 6 deck: it comes from Examples PDF, Exercise 3 (**extension**).

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
- Four measurable indicators, each with its unit or ratio, linked to the objectives of the case: punctuality, data on time, spare parts, customer, adoption.
- The link with controlling: standard, measurement, deviation, corrective action.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
#### Definition and link with controlling

A KPI is a quantified measure of performance against an objective (Examples PDF, Exercise 3; **extension**). It serves the second activity of controlling, measuring actual performance, so that deviations from the standard can be identified and corrected (Topic 6, Slide 24).

#### Four KPIs for Altair MRO

1. **On-time release rate:** percentage of aircraft returned to the airline on or before the promised date (the problem that started the decision).
2. **Digital adoption rate:** percentage of maintenance tasks recorded on the tablet instead of on paper, per hangar and per month.
3. **Spare-part waits:** number of tasks stopped per month because a spare part was missing, which the automatic stock update should reduce.
4. **Customer satisfaction score:** the airlines' rating of the information they receive on the progress of their aircraft, after each maintenance visit.

Other valid KPIs: hours of training completed per technician, number of task cards lost (should fall to zero), average turnaround time per check.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x: Compare what the platform needs (tasks and procedures that change quickly, information shared across departments, decisions taken close to the aircraft) with the coordination, specialization, standardization and centralization of each of the five configurations.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
- Hardest: machine bureaucracy, with its features (rules and formal procedures, routine specialized tasks, functional departmentalization, centralized decisions, many layers, low span of control) matched to the facts of the statement.
- Easiest: adhocracy (low standardization and formalization, decentralization, matrix departmentalization, used for specific projects).
- Functional, divisional or matrix arguments are also accepted when reasoned.

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x:
#### Hardest: machine bureaucracy

The **machine bureaucracy** has a proliferation of rules and very formalized procedures, highly specialized routine tasks, functional departmentalization, centralized decision-making and many layers with a low span of control (Topic 6, Slide 16). Altair MRO already shows these features: procedures "written in detailed manuals", a firm "organized by functions" with a head each, "six hierarchical levels" and every change "approved by the technical director". Every manual must be rewritten, the functional departments must start sharing data they keep separate today, and each change climbs six levels before it is approved, so the platform is hardest to introduce there.

#### Easiest: adhocracy

The **adhocracy (innovative organization)** has low standardization and formalization, decentralization as the key to flexibility, matrix departmentalization and a mix of middle line, operating core and staff, and it is used as a complementary structure for specific projects (Topic 6, Slide 22). A cross-functional project team can test the platform, change it and decide on the spot, so the introduction is easiest there; Altair MRO can use such a team for the pilot in one hangar, as part (a) proposes.

#### The other configurations and alternative answers

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x: The **simple structure** decides quickly by direct supervision but is meant for start-ups and very small firms, not for 600 employees (Topic 6, Slide 15); in a **professional bureaucracy** qualified professionals decide on their own work (Topic 6, Slide 18), and in a **division organization** each division is a bureaucracy that can try the platform on its own (Topic 6, Slide 20). An answer that names a functional structure (departmental silos) as the hardest and a matrix structure as the easiest is also valid if it is reasoned (Examples PDF, Exercise 3): functional departmentalization is a feature of the machine bureaucracy and matrix departmentalization of the adhocracy (Topic 6, Slides 16 and 22).

chunks.t: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
chunks.x: The case uses the whole of Topic 6: the decision is innovative and strategic (Slides 5 and 7), it is taken through the eight-step process (Slide 6), carried out through the four managerial functions (Slides 3-4), checked with indicators that serve controlling (Slide 24), and its difficulty depends on the configuration of the firm (Slides 15-22). The present structure of Altair MRO is close to a machine bureaucracy, so the advice is to pilot the platform in an adhocracy-like project team before extending it to the three hangars.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.h: Bank M05 — Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Case written for the bank in the style of Exercises 2 and 3 of the examples PDF, which has no Topic 7 exercise. Celeris Launch, Vektor Space and Carbotec are fictitious companies. Concepts and definitions: Topic 7, Slides 3-19.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: Celeris Launch is a Spanish start-up founded in 2021 by four engineers who had worked for six years on the guidance of vertically landing vehicles in a university research group. The university's technology transfer office helped them license the guidance software and set up the company, and a private non-profit foundation, which does no research of its own, funded the last two years of the group's landing experiments. Celeris has its plant in an aerospace park where some twenty firms (structures, avionics, test services) share suppliers and customers; several of its engineers came from those neighbouring firms, bringing with them what they had learnt there. The national space agency granted Celeris access to the engine test stand of a government laboratory.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: Celeris's small launcher has a reusable first stage: after separation it restarts its engines, deploys grid fins and landing legs, and lands vertically on a barge, so the stage, its engines and its guidance work together in a way no expendable launcher needs. The firm also 3D-prints the injector of its engine as a single piece instead of machining and brazing forty parts; the injector keeps the same geometry and performance, its production time falls from six weeks to five days, and the printers were already used in the plant for brackets. Finally, Carbotec, a composites supplier of the park, co-developed with Celeris a carbon-fibre interstage that replaces the aluminium one with the same shape and the same interfaces, and is 30% lighter.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: The incumbent, Vektor Space, has built expendable launchers in series for thirty years; its strength is producing single-use stages cheaply, and it has no experience in landing guidance or in refurbishing a stage between flights. Its last three upgrades each cost more than the previous one and raised the payload delivered to orbit per million euros by less than 2%. Celeris's first flights delivered less payload per million euros than Vektor's launcher, but the figure has improved quickly with each landing and reuse. Celeris's chief executive says that "our design will become the standard of the industry as soon as the space agency declares it the official one".

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
| Concept of the course | Definition used | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Product / process innovation | embodied in the outputs (goods or services) / a change in the way the organization conducts its business, such as the techniques of producing | Topic 7, Slide 11 |
| Radical / incremental | very new and different from prior solutions / a relatively minor change to existing practices | Topic 7, Slide 12 |
| Competence-enhancing / destroying | builds on / renders obsolete the existing knowledge and skills of a given firm; it depends on the perspective | Topic 7, Slide 12 |
| Architectural / component | changes the overall design of a system or the way its components interact / changes one or more components without significantly affecting the overall configuration | Topic 7, Slide 13 |
| S-curve of performance | performance against effort: slow, then fast, then flat near the limit of the technology | Topic 7, Slide 14 |
| Discontinuous technology | fulfils a similar market need by building on an entirely new knowledge base | Topic 7, Slide 15 |
| Dominant design | a single architecture with usually 50% or more of the market; a de facto standard, selected through learning effects and network externalities | Topic 7, Slides 17-19 |

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: Take one innovation at a time and ask four questions: is it in the output or in the way of producing? How far is it from prior solutions? Whose knowledge does it use or make obsolete (name the firm)? Does it change the configuration of the system or only one part?

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
- Reusable first stage: product, radical, architectural; competence-destroying for Vektor Space, competence-enhancing for Celeris.
- Printed injector: process, incremental, component; competence-enhancing for Celeris (printers already in use).
- Composite interstage: product, incremental, component; competence-enhancing for Carbotec.
- The competence pair is always stated from the perspective of a named firm.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
#### Reusable first stage

- **Product innovation:** it is embodied in Celeris's output, the launcher and the launch service it sells ("Celeris's small launcher has a reusable first stage") [Topic 7, Slide 11].
- **Radical:** a stage that "restarts its engines, deploys grid fins and landing legs, and lands vertically on a barge" is very new and different from prior solutions, the expendable stages Vektor has built for thirty years [Topic 7, Slide 12].
- **Architectural:** the case says that "the stage, its engines and its guidance work together in a way no expendable launcher needs": the overall design of the vehicle and the way its components interact change [Topic 7, Slide 13].
- **Competence-destroying for Vektor Space,** whose strength is "producing single-use stages cheaply" and which has "no experience in landing guidance or in refurbishing a stage"; **competence-enhancing for Celeris,** whose founders "had worked for six years on the guidance of vertically landing vehicles". The same innovation enhances one firm's competences and destroys another's, as the course stresses [Topic 7, Slide 12].

#### Printed injector

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
- **Process innovation:** "the injector keeps the same geometry and performance"; what changes is the technique of producing it, with a gain in efficiency ("production time falls from six weeks to five days") [Topic 7, Slide 11].
- **Incremental:** the engine and the injector are unchanged and the printers "were already used in the plant for brackets", so it is a relatively minor change to the firm's existing practices [Topic 7, Slide 12].
- **Component:** only one component is affected and the configuration of the engine and of the launcher does not change [Topic 7, Slide 13].
- **Competence-enhancing for Celeris,** because it builds on the printing knowledge it already had. (It would be competence-destroying for a workshop whose skill is machining and brazing the forty parts; the case does not name one, so this remains a remark.)

#### Composite interstage

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
- **Product innovation:** the interstage is part of the launcher Celeris sells [Topic 7, Slide 11].
- **Incremental:** it replaces the aluminium interstage "with the same shape and the same interfaces" and makes it lighter, a relatively minor change to an existing solution [Topic 7, Slide 12].
- **Component:** one component changes without significantly affecting the overall configuration of the system, since the shape and interfaces are kept [Topic 7, Slide 13].
- **Competence-enhancing for Carbotec,** a composites supplier whose existing knowledge base it builds on [Topic 7, Slide 12].

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: Go through the players of Slides 3 and 8 (individuals, firms, universities, government-funded research, private non-profits) and then through the two features of networks of Slide 9.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
- University research and its technology transfer office.
- Government-funded research: the agency and the test stand of a government laboratory.
- A private non-profit that funds the R&D of others without doing its own.
- Firms: Celeris's own R&D and suppliers' technology (Carbotec), a source of development work.
- A technology cluster (the aerospace park) and technological spillovers (engineers moving between firms).
- The linkages among all of them, the most important source of innovation.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
#### Sources of innovation

- **Universities:** the founders come from "a university research group", and "the university's technology transfer office helped them license the guidance software", the role the course gives to these offices: to increase the degree to which university research leads to commercial innovation [Topic 7, Slide 8].
- **Private non-profit organizations:** the foundation "which does no research of its own, funded the last two years of the group's landing experiments", one of the nonprofits that fund the R&D of other organizations without performing it [Topic 7, Slide 8].
- **Government-funded research:** the national space agency gives access to "the engine test stand of a government laboratory" [Topic 7, Slide 8].
- **Firms:** Celeris's own development work, and "Carbotec, a composites supplier ... co-developed" the interstage: suppliers' technology is the third source of development work in the ranking of Slide 6 [Topic 7, Slides 3 and 6].

#### Collaborative networks

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
- **Technology cluster:** the aerospace park where "some twenty firms ... share suppliers and customers" is a regional cluster of firms connected to a common technology, with buyer, supplier and complementary relationships, helped by geographical proximity [Topic 7, Slide 9].
- **Technological spillovers:** engineers who "came from those neighbouring firms, bringing with them what they had learnt there" spread knowledge across organizational boundaries, a positive externality of the R&D of those firms [Topic 7, Slide 9].
- Together, university, nonprofit, agency, laboratory and supplier form the network of linkages that the course calls the most important source of innovation [Topic 7, Slide 4].

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: Read the effect of Vektor's last three upgrades on the S-curve of Slide 14, then compare Celeris's first flights and later flights with the two curves of Slide 15.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
- Vektor: flat upper part of its S-curve, near the limit of the technology (rising cost of each upgrade, gains below 2%).
- Celeris: a discontinuous technology (same market need, entirely new knowledge base) on a second S-curve that starts below and improves quickly.
- Risk for Vektor: the second curve can cross the first; its competences do not carry over.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
#### Vektor's position on its S-curve

Each of Vektor's last three upgrades "cost more than the previous one and raised the payload delivered to orbit per million euros by less than 2%". More effort brings smaller and smaller gains in performance: the expendable technology is in the flat upper part of its S-curve, approaching the limit of the technology [Topic 7, Slide 14].

#### Celeris's technology as a discontinuous technology

Reusable launch fulfils the same market need (putting payloads in orbit) by building on an entirely new knowledge base (landing guidance, engine restart, refurbishment between flights), which makes it a discontinuous technology [Topic 7, Slide 15]. Its curve behaves like the second technology of Slide 15 (b): "Celeris's first flights delivered less payload per million euros than Vektor's launcher", so it starts below, "but the figure has improved quickly with each landing and reuse", so it is in the steep part of its own S-curve.

#### What it means for the incumbent

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: If the trend continues, the second curve crosses Vektor's curve, and further effort on the expendable technology yields little because it is near its limit. Since the new technology is competence-destroying for Vektor (part a), its thirty years of skill in series production of single-use stages do not carry over: to compete it must acquire a new knowledge base rather than keep investing in the old curve.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
- Dominant design: a single architecture with usually 50% or more of the market, a de facto standard.
- Learning effects: each landing and reuse improves the design; revenue reinvested; absorptive capacity.
- Network externalities: installed base and complementary goods (extension of the console example to launchers, stated as such).
- Winner-take-all tendency, with alternatives surviving in niches.
- The chief executive confuses a de facto standard with an officially declared one.

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x:
#### Learning effects

The figure of Celeris "has improved quickly with each landing and reuse": the more the technology is used, the more it is developed and the more efficient it becomes; the sales of each flight generate revenue to reinvest in refining it, and the firm's experience lets it use the technology more productively. Its absorptive capacity, the ability to recognize, assimilate and use new knowledge (here the university guidance research and the knowledge of engineers from the park), speeds this up [Topic 7, Slide 18].

#### Network externalities

The course defines network externalities as an increase in the value of a good to a user with the number of users, through the installed base and complementary goods, with the example of a video game console [Topic 7, Slide 19]. Applied to launchers (an application of the case, **extension** of the course example): the installed base would be the number of customers and satellites already flying on the reusable design, and the complementary goods the payload adapters, integration services and ground support built for it; the more of them there are, the more valuable the design is to the next customer.

#### Dominant design and the chief executive's statement

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: If these forces work, the reusable architecture could reach usually 50% or more of the market and become the dominant design, pushing the market towards winner-take-all, with alternative designs (expendable launchers) surviving in niches [Topic 7, Slides 17 and 19]. The chief executive's claim does not belong to the course's explanation: a dominant design is a **de facto standard**, a standard of the industry even if it is not officially enforced or acknowledged; it is selected by the market through learning effects and network externalities, not by an official declaration of the space agency [Topic 7, Slide 17].

chunks.t: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
chunks.x: The case shows that the pairs of innovation types are not exclusive alternatives for one innovation but four independent questions, and that the competence pair has no answer until the firm is named. The reusable stage is at once product, radical, architectural and competence-destroying for the incumbent, which is why it threatens Vektor far more than the lighter interstage or the printed injector, both incremental component changes.

The newly appointed financial director of **LOGÍSTICA FRIGORÍFICA DEL LEVANTE S.L. (FRIGOLEV)**, a company located in the port area of Castellón and dedicated to the manufacturing of isothermal containers and cold-chain storage equipment for agricultural exporters, is working on the closing of its financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018).

The company was originally incorporated on 1 January 2016 (01/01/2016) by four partners, with an initial contribution of each of 1.500 m.u. disbursed fully in cash at that time, and no further capital modifications took place until fiscal year 2018. Due to the sudden departure of the previous chief accountant, the financial director only has an incomplete balance of the company as of 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), which is included below with certain missing figures marked as (?), along with the audit notes detailing the operations that have taken place during the period from 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018) to 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018):

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
**I.** On 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), the company had as depreciable fixed assets only the industrial refrigeration chambers purchased on a certain date during 2016, which have a useful life of 10 years and are amortized linearly with a residual value of 10% of their acquisition cost. In addition, the balance sheet at 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) reflected an industrial plot of land acquired in 2016 and financial shares of other companies acquired as a permanent investment.

**II.** During the year 2018, the company has sold 3.600 units of isothermal containers at a catalog price of 25 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 300 u.). The general payment condition agreed with the customers implies that this will occur 60 days after the sale. **Hypotheses** (readings of the statement that the solution depends on):
1. Item IV: 75% of the 1.200 m.u. (900 m.u.) is collected; the remaining 25% (300 m.u.) is exactly the 200 m.u. deferred plus the 100 m.u. written off.

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. New sales of the cooperative

$$75 \times 0{,}90 = 67{,}5 \text{ u./month}, \qquad 67{,}5 \times 25 = 1.687{,}5 \text{ m.u./month}, \qquad 12 \times 1.687{,}5 = 20.250 \text{ m.u.}$$

$$\Delta\text{Revenue} = 20.250 - 20.700 = -450 \text{ m.u.} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Revenue} = 87.750 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 2. Raw material (hypothesis 4)

In the base case 4.500 tons were consumed for 3.600 units: $4.500 / 3.600 = 1{,}25$ t/unit $= 2{,}50$ m.u./unit. Selling $12 \times 7{,}5 = 90$ units fewer:

$$\Delta\text{Consumption} = -90 \times 2{,}50 = -225 \text{ m.u.} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{final stock} = 1.800 + 225 = 2.025 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 3. New results

$$\text{Profit before taxes} = 24.000 - 450 + 225 = 23.775, \qquad \text{Tax} = 0{,}25 \times 23.775 = 5.943{,}75$$

$$\text{Net profit} = 23.775 - 5.943{,}75 = 17.831{,}25, \qquad \text{Remaining} = 17.431{,}25$$

$$\text{Reserves} = 0{,}60 \times 17.431{,}25 = 10.458{,}75, \qquad \text{Dividends} = 0{,}40 \times 17.431{,}25 = 6.972{,}50$$

#### Step 4. New cash

The cooperative now pays at 60 days: January to October collected, $10 \times 1.687{,}5 = 16.875$ instead of 20.700 (−3.825). The dividend paid falls by 67,50; the tax is not paid in 2018.

$$\text{Cash} = 14.060 - 3.825 + 67{,}50 = 10.302{,}50 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 5. Changes in the statements

| **Total liabilities and equity** | 38.270 | 38.112,50 | −157,50 |

**Discussion.** The **profit is higher with the discount** (18.000 against 17.831,25): removing the discount gains $2$ m.u. on each of the 810 units the cooperative still buys ($810 \times 2 = 1.620$ m.u.), but the 90 units it stops buying carried a margin over raw material of $23 - 2{,}50 = 20{,}50$ m.u. each ($90 \times 20{,}50 = 1.845$ m.u.); the net effect before taxes is $1.620 - 1.845 = -225$ m.u. The **cash is also higher with the discount** (14.060 against 10.302,50): the cooperative pays in the same month, while under the general condition November and December stay as receivables. Keeping the discount wins on both counts.

chunks.t: FRIGOLEV: an incomplete 2017 balance, a cooperative discount and the 2018 statements
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** units × m.u./unit and tons × m.u./ton give m.u.; m.u./year × months/12 gives m.u.; ratios are dimensionless.
- **Why ROA and ROE are so high:** the company's annual sales (88.200 m.u.) are ten times its 2017 assets; the ratios are measured on the year-end balance, which already includes most of the year's profit.
- **Accrual vs cash:** net profit 18.000 m.u., but cash grew by only 13.120 m.u. because 11.250 m.u. of sales are uncollected, although many expenses (tax, software, raw material, renting) are still unpaid.
- **Typical mistakes:** depreciating the vehicles for 12 months, forgetting the residual values, treating the issue premium as capital, and putting the whole short-term credit or the 200 m.u. deferred receivable outside current items.

To finance the operations of the company, on 1 January 2017 (01/01/2017) a bank granted the company a loan of 1.500 m.u. at 6% annual interest, with a duration of 5 years, i.e. until 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021). Each 31 December, the company must return to the bank an equal principal amount of 300 m.u. and should also pay the due annual interest (6%) calculated from the loan value at the beginning of each year.

During 2017, the company invested in a fleet of agricultural drones worth 2.400 m.u. The useful life of the drones purchased was 8 years (amortized linearly, with no residual value) and at the end of 2017 the company recorded in accumulated depreciation an amount of 75 m.u. for those assets. Also, a further investment of 400 m.u. in mapping software licenses was made on 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) to process aerial images. They use these licenses for 4 years (linear amortization with residual value zero). In addition, the company spent 800 m.u. to purchase a plot of rural land for its flight testing base. Most of 2017 was devoted to obtaining civil aviation permits and only the actual business work was started in the final months of the year. At 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), its balance sheet reflected a loss of 220 m.u., there was no stock (stock in stock) nor pending customer or supplier balances, and the cash in hand and bank account was 1.955 m.u.

**The following information applies to fiscal year 2018:**

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
The external auditor of **TALLERES AERONÁUTICOS DEL HENARES S.A. (TAHSA)**, a company of Alcalá de Henares dedicated to the machining of titanium brackets and fittings for the aircraft structures industry, must issue the audit report on the financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019). The auditor has the balance of the company as of 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018), which is included below, and the following operations that have taken place during the period from 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) to 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019).

**I.** The company has sold during the year 2.400 brackets at a price of 8 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 200 u.). A part of the sales of each month, always the same percentage, is charged in cash in the moment of the sale; the rest is payable to 90 days. Unfortunately the commercial department has lost the contract that fixes this percentage.

**II.** During the first quarter of 2019, the unpaid taxes and the outstanding supplier balances of the previous year were paid. The customer debt outstanding from the previous year was charged in January, except 160 m.u. from an airline component maker declared in insolvency on 1 March 2019 (01/03/2019), which is definitively lost.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**III.** At 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 800 kg of titanium bar valued at 1,50 m.u. / kg. On 1 February 2019 (01/02/2019) the company purchased 3.000 kg at 1,50 m.u. / kg, 50% payable to 60 days and the other 50% deferred until 1 February 2020 (01/02/2020). On 1 August 2019 (01/08/2019) it purchased 2.000 kg more at the same price, payable to 120 days. The count of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) shows 900 kg in the warehouse.

**IV.** Personnel expenses have been 400 m.u. / month (to which 120 m.u. / month must be added for Social Security); salaries are paid in the month in which they are produced and Social Security the month after. General expenses (electricity, insurance, cleaning) amount to 150 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made.

**V.** The machinery of the balance of 2018 was bought on 1 January 2016 (01/01/2016) and is amortized linearly in 10 years with residual value zero. On 1 April 2019 (01/04/2019) the company bought a 5-axis CNC centre that cost 4.800 m.u., paid in full in cash that day. To finance it, the same day a bank granted a loan of 3.600 m.u. at 5% annual interest, to be returned in one single payment on 1 April 2022 (01/04/2022); the interest is paid every 1 April for the year that ends that day. The CNC centre will be amortized linearly in 8 years with a residual value of 480 m.u.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**VI.** The long-term loan of the balance of 2018 bears 4% annual interest. The company returns 300 m.u. of principal every 30 June and every 31 December, paying the same days the interest of the semester calculated on the debt at the beginning of the semester.

**VII.** On 1 October 2019 (01/10/2019) the shareholders subscribed a capital increase of 500 new shares of 2 m.u. nominal value, without issue premium, disbursing that day only 50%; the rest will be called in 2020. On 15 November 2019 (15/11/2019) the company received in cash a dividend of 80 m.u. from its financial shares in AEROPIEZAS S.A., a permanent investment.

**VIII.** The bank statement at 23:00 hrs on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), before any operation of the closing, shows a balance of 3.024 m.u. The results are declared at 23:59 hrs; the corporation tax of 30% is paid immediately, and 50% of the profit after taxes is paid as dividends before the final balance at 24:00 on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019); the rest goes to reserves.

**BALANCE 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018)**

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**Required:**
1. Deduce, justifying it from the bank statement, the percentage of the sales that is charged in cash, and construct the Income Statement (Profit and Loss Account) of TAHSA for the year 2019.
2. Construct and justify the balance sheet at 24:00 on 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), showing all the intermediate calculations.
3. Determine the values of the ROA and ROE ratios in 2019.
4. The commercial director proposes for 2020 that 50% of the sales be charged in cash, granting on those cash sales a discount of 4%. Indicate what changes would have occurred in the Income Statement, the cash and the balance sheet of 2019 if this policy had been applied from 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019). In which case is the profit higher, and in which case is the final cash balance higher? Discuss, reasoned, why.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
**Unknown of the problem:** the share $p$ of each month's sales charged in cash. Every other flow of cash can be computed, so the bank statement before the closing (3.024 m.u.) gives one equation in $p$.

**Collections at 90 days:** a sale of January is collected in April; the sales of October, November and December are still pending at 31/12/2019.

**Uncalled capital:** the shareholders owe the 50% not yet disbursed; it is shown as a deduction of the subscribed capital, as in the Company X exercise of the course.

**Extension (not defined in the course decks).** $\text{ROA} = \text{Income from operations}/\text{Total assets}$ and $\text{ROE} = \text{Net profit}/\text{Owners equity}$, on the balance at 24:00 on 31/12/2019.

chunks.x: Write the cash at 23:00 as initial cash + all inflows − all outflows, leaving the collections from 2019 sales as a function of $p$: $12 \times 1.600\,p + 9 \times 1.600\,(1-p)$.

chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Outflows before the closing

| Suppliers 2018 and unpaid taxes 2018 | $700 + 300$ | 1.000 |

| CNC centre | | 4.800 |
| Old loan: principal | $300 + 300$ | 600 |
| Old loan: interest | $1.800 \times 0{,}04 \times \tfrac{6}{12} + 1.500 \times 0{,}04 \times \tfrac{6}{12} = 36 + 30$ | 66 |
| **Total** | | **19.336** |

#### Step 2. Inflows other than the 2019 sales

$$\underbrace{1.600 - 160}_{\text{2018 receivables}} + \underbrace{3.600}_{\text{new loan}} + \underbrace{0{,}50 \times 1.000}_{\text{capital disbursed}} + \underbrace{80}_{\text{dividend received}} = 1.440 + 3.600 + 500 + 80 = 5.620 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 3. Equation for $p$

Monthly sales are $200 \times 8 = 1.600$ m.u. The cash part of every month is collected (12 months); the credit part only for January to September (9 months):

$$900 + 5.620 + 12 \times 1.600\,p + 9 \times 1.600\,(1 - p) - 19.336 = 3.024$$

$$19.200\,p + 14.400 - 14.400\,p = 3.024 + 19.336 - 900 - 5.620 = 15.840$$

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
$$4.800\,p = 15.840 - 14.400 = 1.440 \;\Rightarrow\; p = \frac{1.440}{4.800} = 0{,}30 = 30\%$$

Collections from 2019 sales: $19.200 \times 0{,}30 + 9 \times 1.120 = 5.760 + 10.080 = 15.840$ m.u.; pending at 31/12: $3 \times 1.120 = 3.360$ m.u.

#### Step 4. Titanium consumed

$$\text{Consumption} = 1.200 + 3.000 \times 1{,}50 + 2.000 \times 1{,}50 - 900 \times 1{,}50 = 1.200 + 4.500 + 3.000 - 1.350 = 7.350 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 5. Depreciation

$$D_{\text{machinery}} = \frac{6.000}{10} = 600 \quad \left(\text{check: } 3 \text{ years} \times 600 = 1.800 \text{ at } 31/12/2018 \;\checkmark\right)$$

$$D_{\text{CNC}} = \frac{4.800 - 480}{8} \times \frac{9}{12} = 540 \times \frac{9}{12} = 405, \qquad D_{2019} = 600 + 405 = 1.005 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 6. Financial items

$$I_{\text{old loan}} = 66 \text{ (Step 1)}, \qquad I_{\text{CNC loan}} = 3.600 \times 0{,}05 \times \frac{9}{12} = 135 \text{ (accrued, paid 01/04/2020)}$$

$$\text{Financial expenses} = 66 + 135 = 201, \qquad \text{Financial income (dividend received)} = 80 \text{ m.u.}$$

#### Step 7. Income Statement 2019

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x: **Discussion.** The **profit is higher with the present policy**: the discount is a real cost of 384 m.u. (269 m.u. after tax). The **cash is higher with the new policy**: 576 m.u. more are collected in 2019 because more of each sale is charged at once, and the lower profit also means less tax and fewer dividends paid at the closing. The discount buys liquidity at the price of profitability; it is worth it only if the company needs the cash or if the money collected earlier earns more than the discount costs.

chunks.t: TAHSA: deducing the share of cash sales from the bank balance
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** units × m.u./unit, kg × m.u./kg and m.u./year × months/12 all give m.u.; $p$ and the ratios are dimensionless.
- **Why the bank balance is enough:** all the other flows are fixed by the terms of the contracts, so the cash balance determines the single unknown term, the share of cash sales.
- **Uncalled capital:** the 500 m.u. not disbursed are a debt of the shareholders to the company, not cash; showing them as a deduction keeps equity at the money actually contributed.
- **Typical mistakes:** paying the CNC loan interest in 2019, depreciating the CNC for 12 months, counting the dividend received as revenue from operations, and treating the bad debt as a collection.

**AVIÓNICA DEL EBRO S.L. (AVIEBRO)**, a Zaragoza workshop dedicated to the repair and calibration of avionics equipment for regional airlines and flying schools, must present to the bank that finances it the financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020). The financial director has the balance of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), included below, and the following operations of the first semester, from 1 January 2020 (01/01/2020) to 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020):

**I.** The company has invoiced repairs for 1.600 m.u. every month. The payment condition agreed with the customers is payable to 60 days. A regional airline, which represents 40% of the invoicing of every month, surpassed in March the annual volume agreed in its contract, and from 1 April 2020 (01/04/2020) it receives a discount of 5% on all its invoices.

**II.** The customer debt outstanding at 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) was charged in January, except 250 m.u. from a flying school that has been granted to pay it on 30 September 2020 (30/09/2020). The suppliers of the previous year were paid in February. As the company closed 2019 with losses, there were no taxes to pay.

**III.** At 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 300 spare parts valued at 2 m.u. / unit. On 1 February 2020 (01/02/2020) the company purchased 400 parts at 2 m.u., 50% paid in cash and 50% payable to 90 days; on 1 May 2020 (01/05/2020) it purchased 300 parts more at the same price, payable to 120 days. At 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020) there remain 250 parts in the warehouse.

The overheads (electricity, telephone, cleaning) are 100 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made. On 1 March 2020 (01/03/2020) the company carried out a renting contract for a test bench of 120 m.u. monthly, paid at the end of each month.

**V.** The patent of the balance (a calibration procedure) is amortized linearly in 5 years with residual value zero; the computer equipment was bought on 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) and is amortized linearly in 3 years with residual value zero.

**VI.** On 1 April 2020 (01/04/2020) AVIEBRO bought a small hangar next to the airport: the building is valued at 2.000 m.u. and the land at 1.000 m.u. chunks.x: **Discussion.** The **profit is higher buying the hangar**: three months of rent (150) cost more than the depreciation of the building (10) and the mortgage interest (24) together, because the land is not depreciated and the mortgage is cheap. The **cash is higher renting**: the company keeps the 600 m.u. of down payment and pays only 150 of rent. Buying gives more profit but ties up cash and adds 2.400 m.u. of debt; renting preserves liquidity, which matters for a workshop that ends the semester with only 538 m.u. in the bank.

chunks.t: AVIEBRO: a half-year close with a volume discount, a mortgage and prior losses
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** m.u./month × months gives m.u.; rates × m.u. × months/12 give m.u.; ratios dimensionless.
- **Half-year ratios:** ROA and ROE of a semester are not annual returns; annualising them would roughly double them.
- **Profit is not cash:** the company earned 1.561,25 m.u. but its cash fell from 700 to 538 m.u.: the hangar, the uncollected May–June invoices and the growth of receivables absorbed it.
- **Typical mistakes:** depreciating the land, applying the airline discount to the whole semester, paying the mortgage interest in the semester, and taxing the profit without offsetting the losses as the statement allows.

The chief financial officer (CFO) of **COMPOSITES AEROESPACIALES DE ÁLAVA S.A. (CAESA)**, a company of Vitoria dedicated to the manufacturing of carbon-fibre fairings for helicopters, is closing the books of the year 2021. The balance of the company at 31 December 2020 (31/12/2020) is included below; the operations of the period from 1 January 2021 (01/01/2021) to 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021) have been the following:

**I.** The company has sold 1.200 fairings at a price of 30 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 100 u.). Of the sales of every month, 20% is charged in cash and the remaining 80% is payable to 60 days. The customer debt of the previous year was charged in January, and the suppliers and the unpaid taxes of the previous year were paid in January and in April respectively.

**II.** At 31 December 2020 (31/12/2020) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 500 kg of epoxy resin valued at 3 m.u. / kg. On 1 March 2021 (01/03/2021) the company purchased 4.000 kg at 3 m.u. / kg, paying 30% in cash and the remaining 70% in two equal parts, on 1 September 2021 (01/09/2021) and on 1 March 2022 (01/03/2022). At 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021) there remain 700 kg in the warehouse.

chunks.t: CAESA: financing a second autoclave with a semiannual loan or with new shares
chunks.x:
**III.** The fixed salaries are 1.000 m.u. / month, paid in the same month, to which 300 m.u. / month of Social Security must be added, paid the month after. Variable wages of the lamination staff amounted in 2021 to 1.200 m.u. (paid in cash). The external supplies (energy for the autoclaves) are 250 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made.

**IV.** The autoclave of the balance was bought on 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018) and is amortized linearly in 10 years with a residual value of 1.000 m.u. On 1 July 2021 (01/07/2021) CAESA put into service a second autoclave of 6.000 m.u. (amortized linearly in 10 years with a residual value of 600 m.u.) together with a software license for the control of the curing cycles of 1.200 m.u. (amortized linearly in 3 years with residual value zero), both paid in full in cash that day.

**V.** To pay the 7.200 m.u. of the expansion, the board accepted on 1 July 2021 (01/07/2021) a bank loan of 7.200 m.u. at 5% annual interest, to be returned in 8 semiannual installments of 900 m.u. every 1 January and every 1 July, the first on 1 January 2022 (01/01/2022); the same days the company pays the interest of the semester calculated on the debt at the beginning of the semester. The long-term loan of the balance bears 6% annual interest, paid every 31 December, and is returned in one single payment on 31 December 2023 (31/12/2023).

**VII.** The alternative rejected by the board was a capital increase on 1 July 2021 (01/07/2021) of 4.800 new shares of 1 m.u. nominal value with an issue premium of 50% over the nominal value, fully disbursed in cash, instead of the bank loan.
